topics.title: Fuels and combustion
points: Exothermic reactions release energy (\(\Delta H < 0\)); endothermic reactions absorb it (\(\Delta H > 0\)).
Fossil fuels (coal, crude oil, natural gas) are non-renewable. Biofuels (bioethanol, biogas, biodiesel) are renewable but need land, water and energy to make.
Complete combustion: fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Incomplete combustion (little O₂) also makes CO and soot, and releases less energy.
Thermochemical equations show \(\Delta H\) for the moles in the equation: \[\mathrm{CH_4(g) + 2O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g) + 2H_2O(l)} \quad \Delta H = -890\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\]
Heat of combustion is given in \(\mathrm{kJ\ g^{-1}}\) or \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) in the data book: \(E = n \times \Delta H_c\) or \(E = m \times (\mathrm{kJ\ g^{-1}})\).
Bioethanol from fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. It is carbon neutral only in theory, because farming and processing release CO₂.

qs.q: Ethanol has a molar heat of combustion of 1360 kJ mol⁻¹ and M = 46.0. What is its heat of combustion in kJ g⁻¹?
Methane releases 890 kJ mol⁻¹ when burnt. How much energy is released by burning [[m]] g of methane (M = 16.0 g mol⁻¹)? Give a whole number.

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with moles, balancing equations (including combustion) and the families of organic compounds from Units 1 and 2.

The big idea: fuels store chemical energy, and burning them releases it. To choose between fuels you need to measure how much energy each releases, and weigh that against where the fuel comes from and what it emits. This lesson gives you the vocabulary and the equations; the next shows how the energy is measured.

Breaking bonds absorbs energy and forming bonds releases it. In an exothermic reaction more energy is released forming the products’ bonds than was absorbed breaking the reactants’ bonds, so the products have lower chemical energy and \(\Delta H\) is negative. Combustion is always exothermic. An energy profile diagram shows the energy of reactants and products, the activation energy and \(\Delta H\).

fig.cap: Energy profile for an exothermic reaction: the products are lower than the reactants, so ΔH is negative. Eₐ is the climb to the transition state.

p: A fuel is a substance with stored chemical energy that can be released relatively easily. Fossil fuels formed from ancient organisms over millions of years and are non-renewable. Biofuels come from recently living matter and can be replaced within a short time: bioethanol from fermenting sugars, biodiesel from fats and oils, and biogas from the breakdown of organic waste without oxygen.

When comparing, consider energy content, whether the source is renewable, greenhouse gas and pollutant emissions over the whole life cycle, land and water use, and cost. Biofuels are close to carbon neutral only in principle: the CO₂ released was recently absorbed by the plants, but farming, processing and transport add emissions.

p: The \(\Delta H\) value belongs to the equation as written, in the states shown. Doubling the coefficients doubles \(\Delta H\); reversing the equation changes its sign.
Example: \(\mathrm{CH_4(g) + 2O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g) + 2H_2O(l)}\), \(\Delta H = -890\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). Burning 2 mol of methane releases 1780 kJ.
check: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for 4NH₃(g) → 2N₂(g) + 6H₂(g)?
Reversing changes the sign and doubling doubles the value: +184 kJ mol⁻¹.

p: How much energy is released when 5.00 g of ethanol (M = 46.0 g mol⁻¹, molar heat of combustion 1360 kJ mol⁻¹) burns completely? What mass of CO₂ forms?

\(n = \dfrac{5.00}{46.0} = 0.109\ \mathrm{mol}\). Energy \(= 0.109 \times 1360 = 148\ \mathrm{kJ}\). \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2 + 3H_2O}\), so \(n(\mathrm{CO_2}) = 0.217\ \mathrm{mol}\) and \(m = 0.217 \times 44.0 = 9.57\ \mathrm{g}\).

Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are oxidised in cellular respiration to release energy. Glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l). Fats release roughly twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates because they contain less oxygen, so more of the molecule can be oxidised.
Complete combustion of any fuel containing C, H and possibly O gives only CO₂ and H₂O. Balance carbon first, then hydrogen, then oxygen, remembering to count any oxygen already in the fuel.
Octane: 2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l). Ethanol: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l). Hydrogen: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l).

Incomplete combustion happens when oxygen is limited. Carbon monoxide or carbon (soot) forms in place of some CO₂, and less energy is released. Example: 2CH₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO(g) + 4H₂O(l). Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen.
check: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of propan-1-ol, C₃H₇OH.
2C₃H₇OH(l) + 9O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 8H₂O(l).

notes.h: Energy per mole, per gram and per litre
p: The data book gives molar heats of combustion in kJ mol⁻¹. To compare fuels by mass, divide by the molar mass. Methane: \(\dfrac{890}{16.0} = 55.6\ \mathrm{kJ\ g^{-1}}\). Ethanol: \(\dfrac{1360}{46.0} = 29.6\ \mathrm{kJ\ g^{-1}}\). Ethanol releases less energy per gram because it is already partly oxidised: it contains an oxygen atom.

For liquid fuels, energy per litre matters for storage: multiply the energy per gram by the density in g L⁻¹. Hydrogen has the highest energy per gram of any fuel (about 141 kJ g⁻¹) but, as a gas, a very low energy per litre, which is why storing it is a challenge.
check: Propane has a molar heat of combustion of 2220 kJ mol⁻¹ and a molar mass of 44.0 g mol⁻¹. What is its heat of combustion in kJ g⁻¹?

p: Example: which releases more CO₂ per kJ of energy, methane or octane? Methane: 1 mol gives 1 mol CO₂ and 890 kJ, so \(\dfrac{44.0}{890} = 0.0494\ \mathrm{g\ kJ^{-1}}\). Octane (heat of combustion 5460 kJ mol⁻¹): 1 mol gives 8 mol CO₂, so \(\dfrac{8 \times 44.0}{5460} = 0.0645\ \mathrm{g\ kJ^{-1}}\). Natural gas emits less CO₂ for the same energy.

Photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, is endothermic and stores solar energy in plants. Respiration and the combustion of biofuels release it again. That is the basis for describing biofuels as renewable.

Leaving out the negative sign on an exothermic ΔH, or adding a sign to “energy released”. Writing H₂O(g) when the data book value assumes liquid water. Calling biofuels carbon neutral without qualification.

topics.title: Stoichiometry and calorimetry
points: Gas volumes: \(n = \dfrac{V}{V_m}\) (\(V_m = 24.8\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}}\) at SLC) or \(pV = nRT\).
Limiting reactant decides how much product and energy is released.
Heat absorbed by water: \(q = mc\Delta T\), with \(c = 4.18\ \mathrm{J\ g^{-1}\,{}^\circ C^{-1}}\).
Calorimeters are calibrated electrically: \(\mathrm{CF} = \dfrac{VIt}{\Delta T}\) (\(\mathrm{J\,{}^\circ C^{-1}}\)). Then \(E = \mathrm{CF} \times \Delta T\).
Solution calorimetry: \(\Delta H = -\dfrac{q}{n}\) (negative when the temperature rises).
Bomb calorimeters measure combustion energy; heat losses make experimental values lower than data book values.

qs.q: Heating [[m]] g of water raises its temperature by [[dT]] °C. Find the energy absorbed in kJ (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹), to 2 decimal places.
Burning [[mf]] g of a fuel heats [[m]] g of water by [[dT]] °C. Find the energy released per gram of fuel (kJ g⁻¹), to 1 decimal place. Assume no heat loss.

p: Before this lesson you should know q = mcΔT and thermochemical equations (previous lesson), and be confident with moles.

The big idea: we cannot measure the energy in a chemical bond directly, but we can let a reaction heat some water and measure the temperature change. Calorimetry is the set of techniques for doing that well, and for working out how far an experimental value is from the true one.

Calorimetry measures the energy change of a reaction by the temperature change it causes in a known mass of water or in a calibrated calorimeter. The simplest method burns a fuel under a can of water. Much of the heat escapes, so the result is too low.
Burning 0.500 g of ethanol heats 200 g of water by 15.0 °C. Find the experimental heat of combustion in kJ g⁻¹ and compare it with 29.6 kJ g⁻¹.

\(q = mc\Delta T = 200 \times 4.18 \times 15.0 = 12\,540\ \mathrm{J} = 12.5\ \mathrm{kJ}\). Per gram: \(\dfrac{12.5}{0.500} = 25.1\ \mathrm{kJ\ g^{-1}}\). Efficiency of energy transfer \(= \dfrac{25.1}{29.6} \times 100 = 85\%\). The difference is heat lost to the air and the container, and incomplete combustion.

A calorimeter’s calibration factor is the energy needed to raise its temperature by 1 °C. Electrical calibration passes a known current at a known voltage for a known time: \(E = VIt\) and \(\mathrm{CF} = \dfrac{VIt}{\Delta T}\). Chemical calibration uses a reaction with a known \(\Delta H\). Then for the reaction being studied, \(q = \mathrm{CF} \times \Delta T\).
Solution calorimeters suit reactions in water such as dissolving and neutralisation. Bomb calorimeters are sealed, pressurised with oxygen and surrounded by water; they suit combustion.
check: A calorimeter is calibrated with 6.00 V and 2.00 A for 100 s and the temperature rises 1.50 °C. Find the calibration factor.

p: A calorimeter is calibrated with 4.00 V and 1.50 A for 120 s, giving a rise of 0.850 °C. Then 1.00 g of glucose (M = 180.0) is burned and the temperature rises 18.4 °C.

In a poorly insulated calorimeter the temperature begins to fall before the reaction finishes, so the highest reading understates the true rise. Extrapolate the cooling line back to the time the reaction started to estimate the temperature change that would have occurred with no heat loss.

fig.cap: A temperature–time graph. Heat loss means the highest reading (dashed) understates the rise; extrapolating the cooling line back to the start gives the true ΔT.

p: A thermochemical equation links moles to energy, so energy can be treated like another product. Example: how much energy is released when 100 g of propane burns? \(\mathrm{C_3H_8 + 5O_2 \rightarrow 3CO_2 + 4H_2O},\ \Delta H = -2220\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). \(n = \dfrac{100}{44.0} = 2.27\ \mathrm{mol}\). Energy \(= 2.27 \times 2220 = 5.05 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{kJ}\).

Working backwards: what mass of methane must burn to heat 1.00 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C, if no heat is lost? \(q = 1000 \times 4.18 \times 80 = 334\ \mathrm{kJ}\). \(n = \dfrac{334}{890} = 0.376\ \mathrm{mol}\), so \(m = 0.376 \times 16.0 = 6.01\ \mathrm{g}\). In practice more is needed because heat is lost.
check: The molar heat of combustion of hydrogen is 286 kJ mol⁻¹. How much energy is released by burning 10.0 g of H₂ (M = 2.0)?
n = 5.0 mol, so energy = 5.0 × 286 = 1430 kJ, or 1.43 × 10³ kJ.

p: 50.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of 1.00 M NaOH in an insulated cup. The temperature rises from 21.0 °C to 27.8 °C. Find the enthalpy of neutralisation.

Total mass of solution ≈ 100 g (assuming the density of water). \(q = 100 \times 4.18 \times 6.8 = 2842\ \mathrm{J} = 2.84\ \mathrm{kJ}\). \(n(\mathrm{H_2O\ formed}) = 0.0500 \times 1.00 = 0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(\Delta H = -\dfrac{2.84}{0.0500} = -56.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).
Assumptions to state: the solution has the same density and specific heat capacity as water; no heat is lost to the surroundings or absorbed by the cup.
check: Dissolving a salt lowers the temperature of the water. Is ΔH positive or negative?
Positive. The reaction absorbed heat from the water, so it is endothermic.

notes.h: Why calibrate, and how good is the result?
p: Using q = mcΔT assumes only the water is heated. In a real calorimeter the container, stirrer and thermometer also absorb energy, and some escapes. Calibrating with a known amount of energy measures how the whole apparatus responds, so these effects are built into the calibration factor.

Typical exam prompts: if the calorimeter is poorly insulated during calibration, the measured ΔT is too small, so the calibration factor comes out too large. If heat is lost during the reaction being studied, ΔT is too small and the calculated energy is too low. Always trace the error through the formula step by step.
Using the mass of the fuel as m in q = mcΔT; m is the mass of water. Forgetting to convert J to kJ. Stating the sign of ΔH wrongly: a temperature rise means exothermic and negative.

topics.title: Redox, galvanic cells and fuel cells
points: Oxidation numbers track electron transfer; balance complex half equations with H₂O, H⁺ and e⁻ (KOHES).
The electrochemical series: strongest oxidising agent top left (F₂), strongest reducing agent bottom right (Li). A reaction occurs between an oxidant and a reductant below it.
Galvanic cell: anode (\(-\)) oxidation, cathode (\(+\)) reduction. \(E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\)
Primary cells are not rechargeable. Predictions from E° values assume standard conditions and say nothing about rate.
Fuel cells continuously convert chemical energy to electrical energy; reactants are supplied constantly. Hydrogen fuel cell: H₂ is oxidised at the anode, O₂ reduced at the cathode.
In acidic electrolyte: anode H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O.

qs.a: It completes the circuit and keeps each half-cell electrically neutral by allowing ions to move between them.

qs.q: In a galvanic cell the cathode half-cell has E° = [[a]] V and the anode half-cell has E° = [[b]] V. Find the cell voltage under standard conditions.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to assign oxidation numbers, balance half-equations in acid and describe a simple galvanic cell (Unit 2 redox).

The big idea: a spontaneous redox reaction releases energy. If the oxidation and the reduction are kept in separate places, the electrons must flow through a wire, and the energy comes out as electricity. The electrochemical series lets you predict which reactions are spontaneous, which electrode is which, and the voltage.

The series lists half-equations as reductions, in order of E° from most positive at the top to most negative at the bottom. Oxidising agents are on the left; the strongest is at the top left. Reducing agents are on the right; the strongest is at the bottom right.

A spontaneous reaction occurs when the oxidising agent is above the reducing agent on the series, that is, the reactants are top left and bottom right. The higher half-equation runs forward as reduction; the lower one runs in reverse as oxidation.

p: A cell is built from Ag⁺/Ag (E° = +0.80 V) and Zn²⁺/Zn (E° = −0.76 V) half-cells.

Ag⁺ is the stronger oxidising agent, so it is reduced at the cathode (+): Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s). Zinc is oxidised at the anode (−): Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. Overall: Zn(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s). Electrons flow from zinc to silver through the wire.
\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = 0.80 - (-0.76) = 1.56\ \mathrm{V}\). Do not multiply E° values when you multiply a half-equation.
check: A cell uses Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34 V) and Ni²⁺/Ni (−0.25 V). What is the cell voltage and which electrode is the anode?
0.34 − (−0.25) = 0.59 V. Nickel is the anode: it is the stronger reducing agent and is oxidised.

p: E° values apply at standard conditions: 25 °C, 100 kPa and 1 M solutions. Under other conditions the order can change. The series also says nothing about rate: a reaction predicted to be spontaneous may be too slow to observe.

A fuel cell is a galvanic cell in which the reactants are supplied continuously, so it produces electricity for as long as fuel is supplied. The electrodes are porous, to give a large surface area and let gases reach the electrolyte, and contain catalysts to increase the reaction rate. Compared with burning the fuel to drive a turbine, a fuel cell converts chemical energy directly to electrical energy with fewer energy transformations, so it is more efficient.

Hydrogen fuel cell overall: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l). The only product at the point of use is water. The environmental benefit depends on how the hydrogen was produced. Challenges include the cost of catalysts and safe storage and distribution of hydrogen.
Designing cells with renewable feedstocks, less hazardous materials and better energy efficiency applies green chemistry principles. Using cells that can be recycled supports a circular economy.

A half-cell contains both members of a conjugate redox pair, such as Zn²⁺(aq)/Zn(s). Three types appear: a metal electrode in a solution of its ions; an inert electrode (platinum or graphite) in a solution containing both ions of a pair, such as Fe³⁺(aq)/Fe²⁺(aq); and a gas bubbled over an inert electrode, such as Cl₂(g)/Cl⁻(aq). Inert electrodes are used when neither member of the pair is a solid conductor.

Standard electrode potentials are measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, H⁺(aq)/H₂(g), which is assigned 0.00 V. A half-cell above it on the series has a greater tendency to be reduced than H⁺.

Method: list every species actually present. Find each on the series and decide whether it can act as an oxidising agent (left side) or a reducing agent (right side). A reaction occurs if an oxidising agent is higher on the series than a reducing agent.
Example: will copper metal react with silver nitrate solution? Ag⁺ (oxidising agent, +0.80 V) is above Cu (reducing agent, +0.34 V), so yes: Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s).

Example: will copper react with dilute hydrochloric acid? The oxidising agent H⁺ (0.00 V) is below the reducing agent Cu (+0.34 V), so no reaction. Example: can an iron container store nickel(II) sulfate solution? Ni²⁺ (−0.25 V) is above Fe (−0.44 V), so the iron would be oxidised; it is not suitable.
check: Will zinc metal react with a solution of iron(II) sulfate? (Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V; Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V)
Yes. The oxidising agent Fe²⁺ is higher on the series than the reducing agent Zn: Zn(s) + Fe²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Fe(s).

p: A primary cell is a galvanic cell that is discarded when its reactants are used up; the products move away from the electrodes or the reaction cannot be reversed. To analyse an unfamiliar cell, use the half-equations supplied: the oxidation occurs at the anode (negative), the reduction at the cathode (positive), electrons flow from anode to cathode in the external circuit, and ions move in the electrolyte to balance the charge, with anions moving toward the anode.

notes.h: Fuel cells in acidic and alkaline electrolytes
p: Acidic electrolyte. Anode: H₂(g) → 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. Cathode: O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O(l). Alkaline electrolyte. Anode: H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻. Cathode: O₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻(aq). The overall reaction is the same in both: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l).

For a fuel such as methanol in acid: CH₃OH(aq) + H₂O(l) → CO₂(g) + 6H⁺(aq) + 6e⁻ at the anode. Balance with KOHES as usual. The oxidation half-equation always involves the fuel; oxygen is always reduced at the cathode.
check: In a hydrogen fuel cell, at which electrode does hydrogen react, and what is its polarity?
At the anode, where it is oxidised. In a galvanic cell the anode is negative.

topics.title: Rates of reaction
points: Collision theory: particles must collide with enough energy (at least the activation energy) and the right orientation.
Rate increases with higher concentration or pressure (more frequent collisions), greater surface area, and higher temperature.
Temperature increases rate mainly because a larger fraction of collisions have energy \(\geq E_a\) (see the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution).
Catalysts provide an alternative pathway with lower activation energy \(E_a\). They are not used up and do not change \(\Delta H\) or the equilibrium position.
Energy profile diagrams show reactants, products, \(E_a\) and \(\Delta H\).

it has a larger surface area, so more collisions

qs.q: Explain why increasing temperature increases the rate of a reaction.
qs.a: Particles have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and, more importantly, a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.

qs.q: A catalyst increases the rate of reaction by…

qs.q: Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction.
qs.a: Particles move faster, so they collide more often, and a much greater proportion of collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy.

qs.q: A reaction has Eₐ = 75 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −40 kJ mol⁻¹. Find Eₐ for the reverse reaction.
Adding a catalyst to a reversible reaction changes the equilibrium yield by…
qs.e: It speeds up both directions equally.

p: Before this lesson you should understand exothermic and endothermic reactions and energy profile diagrams.

The big idea: for particles to react they must collide hard enough and in the right way. Anything that makes successful collisions more frequent makes the reaction faster. This single model explains every factor that affects rate, and it is how chemists speed up the reactions they want.

For a reaction to happen, particles must collide, with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, and in a suitable orientation. Most collisions are unsuccessful. Reaction rate depends on the number of successful collisions per second.

Concentration or gas pressure: more particles in a given volume, so collisions are more frequent. Surface area of a solid: more particles are exposed, so collisions are more frequent. Temperature: particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent, but the main effect is that a much greater proportion of collisions have energy at or above the activation energy. Catalyst: provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.
A full explanation names the change, says what it does to the frequency or the proportion of successful collisions, and concludes about the rate.

The curve shows how many particles have each kinetic energy. The area under the curve is the total number of particles, and the area to the right of the activation energy is the number able to react. Raising the temperature flattens the curve and moves its peak to the right, with the same total area, so a larger area lies beyond the activation energy. Adding a catalyst leaves the curve unchanged and moves the activation energy line to the left.

fig.cap: Kinetic energy distributions at two temperatures. At the higher temperature, a much larger area (shaded) lies beyond the activation energy.

p: A catalyst is not consumed, so it does not appear in the overall equation and a small amount can be used repeatedly. It lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount. It does not change ΔH, and it does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield. Its value in industry is that acceptable rates can be reached at lower temperatures, saving energy.
check: Does a catalyst change ΔH?
No. It lowers the activation energy by providing an alternative pathway, but the energies of the reactants and products are unchanged.

p: Rate is the change in amount of a reactant or product per unit time. It can be followed by the volume of gas produced, the loss of mass as a gas escapes, a colour change or a change in pH. On a graph of amount against time, a steeper gradient means a faster rate; the curve flattens as reactants are used up, and levels off when the limiting reactant runs out.

On an energy profile, the activation energy \(E_a\) is the gap from the reactants up to the peak. The peak is the transition state, where old bonds are partly broken and new ones partly formed. \(\Delta H\) is the gap from reactants to products. For the reverse reaction, \(E_a(\text{reverse}) = E_a(\text{forward}) - \Delta H\).

Example: a reaction has \(E_a = 120\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) and \(\Delta H = -80\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). The activation energy of the reverse reaction is \(120 - (-80) = 200\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). A catalyst that lowers the forward value to 90 lowers the reverse value to 170; \(\Delta H\) is unchanged.
check: A reaction has Eₐ = 50 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = +30 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?

p: Question: explain why powdered zinc reacts faster with acid than a lump of the same mass. Answer: “The powder has a much greater surface area, so more zinc atoms are exposed to the acid. Collisions between H⁺ ions and zinc atoms are more frequent, so there are more successful collisions per second and the rate is higher.”

Question: explain why raising the temperature by 10 °C can roughly double the rate. Answer: “At the higher temperature the particles have greater average kinetic energy. Collisions are slightly more frequent, but more importantly a much greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so the frequency of successful collisions increases markedly.”

For the volume of gas produced against time: the gradient at any point is the rate. The initial gradient is steepest, because the reactant concentration is highest. The curve flattens as the reactant is used up and becomes horizontal when the reaction is complete. The final height depends only on the amount of limiting reactant.

Compare two experiments. Same amounts but higher temperature or a catalyst: steeper curve, same final height. Half the amount of limiting reactant: half the final height. More concentrated acid in excess with the same mass of metal: steeper curve, same final height, because the metal is limiting.
check: A catalyst is added to a reaction producing a gas. How does the graph of gas volume against time change?
The curve is steeper at the start and levels off sooner, but it reaches the same final volume, because the amount of limiting reactant has not changed.

fig.cap: Gas produced over time. A catalyst gives a steeper start but the same final volume, because the amount of limiting reactant is unchanged.

p: Saying a catalyst “gives particles more energy”. Saying temperature only makes collisions more frequent. Saying a higher concentration gives particles more energy. Confusing rate (how fast) with yield (how much).

topics.title: Equilibrium and Le Chatelier
points: Dynamic equilibrium in a closed system: forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations stay constant.

For \(a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D}\): \[K = \frac{[\mathrm{C}]^c[\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a[\mathrm{B}]^b}\] (no solids or liquid water). \(K\) depends only on temperature.
Large \(K\) (above about \(10^4\)): mostly products. Small \(K\): mostly reactants. Compare the reaction quotient \(Q\) with \(K\) to predict the direction.
Le Chatelier: a system partially opposes a change. Adding reactant shifts right; increasing pressure shifts to the side with fewer gas particles.
Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction (\(K\) changes). Catalysts do not shift equilibrium.
Reversing an equation gives \(\dfrac{1}{K}\); doubling the coefficients gives \(K^2\).
topics.explain: Explain why adding a catalyst does not change the yield at equilibrium.

qs.q: Write the expression for \(K\): \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)}\)
For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH negative), what increases the yield of NH₃?
qs.e: 4 gas particles → 2: higher pressure favours fewer particles.

qs.q: If \(Q < K\), the reaction will…
qs.e: It makes more products until \(Q = K\).

qs.q: \(K\) for \(\mathrm{A} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{B}\) is \(4.0\). What is \(K\) for \(\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{A}\)?
Write the expression for K for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
For A(g) ⇌ 2B(g), equilibrium concentrations are [A] = 0.20 M and [B] = 0.40 M. Find K.
Adding more reactant to a system at equilibrium causes…
If the reaction quotient Q is greater than K, which way does the reaction proceed?
qs.a: In the reverse direction, until Q falls to K.

qs.q: For \(\text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI}(g)\), at equilibrium \([\text{H}_2] = [[a]]\) M, \([\text{I}_2] = [[b]]\) M and \([\text{HI}] = [[c]]\) M. Find \(K_c\), to 1 decimal place.

p: Before this lesson you should understand reaction rate and collision theory, and be confident with concentration calculations.

The big idea: many reactions do not go to completion. They run in both directions at once until the two directions balance. The equilibrium constant tells you where that balance lies, and Le Chatelier’s principle tells you how it moves when conditions change. Industry uses both to get as much product as possible.

In a closed system a reversible reaction reaches a state where the forward and reverse reactions are happening at the same rate. Concentrations then stay constant, although both reactions continue. Equilibrium does not mean the amounts of reactants and products are equal.

For \(a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D}\), \(K = \dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]^c[\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a[\mathrm{B}]^b}\) using equilibrium concentrations. Only a change in temperature changes the value of K. The reaction quotient Q uses the same expression with the concentrations at any moment: if Q is less than K the reaction proceeds forward; if Q is greater than K it proceeds in reverse.
2.0 mol of N₂O₄ is placed in a 1.0 L vessel. At equilibrium 0.80 mol of NO₂ is present. N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). Find K.

Initial: \([\mathrm{N_2O_4}] = 2.0\), \([\mathrm{NO_2}] = 0\). Change: \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) rose by 0.80, so \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}\) fell by 0.40. Equilibrium: \([\mathrm{N_2O_4}] = 1.6\), \([\mathrm{NO_2}] = 0.80\). \(K = \dfrac{0.80^2}{1.6} = 0.40\ \mathrm{M}\).

When a change is made to a system at equilibrium, the system shifts to partially oppose the change. Adding a reactant: the forward reaction is favoured, using some of what was added. Removing a product: the forward reaction is favoured. Decreasing the volume (raising the pressure): the system shifts to the side with fewer gas particles. Adding water to an aqueous equilibrium: shifts to the side with more dissolved particles. Raising the temperature: the endothermic direction is favoured, and K changes. Adding a catalyst or an inert gas at constant volume: no shift.
“Partially” matters. If a reactant is added, its concentration ends up higher than before the change, even though some has reacted.
check: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), ΔH > 0, what happens to the amount of NO₂ when the mixture is cooled?
The system favours the exothermic (reverse) direction, so the amount of NO₂ decreases and K decreases.

p: For an exothermic reaction, a low temperature gives a high equilibrium yield but a slow rate. Industry uses a moderate (compromise) temperature with a catalyst. High pressure improves yield where there are fewer gas particles on the product side, and it also increases rate, but it costs more in equipment and energy. Removing product and recycling unreacted gases improves overall yield and atom economy.

Start with only reactants. The forward reaction is fast at first, because reactant concentrations are high, and slows as they are used. The reverse reaction starts at zero and speeds up as products build up. Eventually the two rates are equal. From then on, concentrations do not change, although both reactions continue. On a concentration–time graph the lines become horizontal; on a rate–time graph the two lines meet.
The same equilibrium position is reached whether you start from the reactants or from the products, provided the temperature is the same.

fig.cap: Starting with reactants only: the forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they are equal, at equilibrium.

notes.h: Calculating and using K: more examples
p: Example 1: for \(\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\), an equilibrium mixture in a 2.0 L vessel contains 0.40 mol H₂, 0.40 mol I₂ and 2.8 mol HI. Concentrations: 0.20, 0.20 and 1.4 M. \(K = \dfrac{1.4^2}{0.20 \times 0.20} = 49\). There are no units here because they cancel. Always convert moles to concentrations first.

Example 2: using Q. For the same reaction at the same temperature, a mixture has \([\mathrm{H_2}] = [\mathrm{I_2}] = 0.50\ \mathrm{M}\) and \([\mathrm{HI}] = 1.0\ \mathrm{M}\). \(Q = \dfrac{1.0^2}{0.25} = 4.0\). Since \(Q < K\), the forward reaction is favoured until Q rises to 49.
Example 3: units. For \(\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3}\), \(K = \dfrac{[\mathrm{NH_3}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2}][\mathrm{H_2}]^3}\) has units \(\mathrm{M^{-2}}\).
check: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), write the expression for K.
K = [SO₃]² ÷ ([SO₂]²[O₂]).

notes.h: Explaining a shift with collision theory
p: Le Chatelier’s principle predicts the direction; rates explain it. Adding a reactant raises its concentration, so the forward reaction becomes faster than the reverse. More product forms, which speeds up the reverse reaction, until the rates are equal again at new concentrations.

Halving the volume doubles all gas concentrations. The reaction with more reacting particles speeds up more, so the net change is toward the side with fewer gas particles. Raising the temperature speeds up both reactions, but the endothermic direction speeds up more, so K changes.

A substance added or removed: a vertical jump in that one line, then all lines curve to new levels. Volume change: all gas concentrations jump together (up for compression), then adjust. Temperature change: no jump; all lines curve gradually from the moment of change. Catalyst added to a system at equilibrium: no change at all. The amounts by which the lines move during the adjustment follow the mole ratio of the equation.
check: On a concentration–time graph, all the lines begin to curve at the same moment with no sudden jump. What change was made?
The temperature was changed.

fig.cap: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. At 10 min extra H₂ is added (a jump); the system partially opposes the change: H₂ and I₂ fall and HI rises to new equilibrium levels.

p: Ammonia: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Yield is favoured by low temperature (exothermic) and high pressure (four gas particles become two). Rate is favoured by high temperature, high pressure and a catalyst. The process uses a moderate temperature of about 400 to 450 °C as a compromise, high pressure, an iron catalyst, removal of ammonia by cooling it to a liquid, and recycling of unreacted gases.

Including solids or pure liquids in K. Saying K changes when concentration or pressure changes. Saying equilibrium shifts “to oppose the change completely”. On concentration–time graphs, drawing a sudden jump for a temperature change: only adding or removing a substance, or changing the volume, gives a sudden jump.

topics.title: Electrolysis and Faraday’s laws
points: Electrolytic cells use electrical energy to drive non-spontaneous reactions. Anode (+) oxidation, cathode (−) reduction.
Predict products using the strongest oxidant (reduced at cathode) and strongest reductant (oxidised at anode) present, including water.
Molten electrolysis avoids water competing; aqueous electrolysis often produces H₂ or O₂ from water.
\(Q = It\) (charge in coulombs). \(n(e^-) = \dfrac{Q}{F}\), where \(F = 96\,500\ \mathrm{C\ mol^{-1}}\).
Rechargeable batteries act as galvanic cells when discharging and electrolytic cells when recharging.
Green hydrogen: electrolysis of water powered by renewable electricity.
topics.explain: Compare the polarity of the electrodes in galvanic and electrolytic cells.

qs.q: A current of \(2.00\ \mathrm{A}\) runs for \(965\ \mathrm{s}\) through \(\mathrm{CuSO_4(aq)}\). What mass of copper forms? (\(M = 63.5\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\))
qs.e: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

qs.q: In an electrolytic cell, the anode is…
Electrolysis of molten NaCl produces…
qs.e: No water present.

qs.q: What makes hydrogen “green”?
qs.a: It is made by electrolysis of water using electricity from renewable sources, so no CO₂ is released in production.

qs.q: What mass of silver is deposited by a current of 0.50 A for 1930 s? (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag; M = 107.9)
In an electrolytic cell, the cathode is…
What are the products when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed?
qs.a: Sodium at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode.

qs.q: Why is sodium not produced when aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed?
qs.a: Water is a stronger oxidising agent than Na⁺, so water is reduced to hydrogen at the cathode instead.

qs.q: A current of [[I]] A flows for [[t]] minutes through \(\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)\). What mass of copper is deposited? (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹, M(Cu) = 63.5.) Give 2 decimal places.

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with galvanic cells and the electrochemical series.

The big idea: electricity can force a chemical reaction to run backwards, in the non-spontaneous direction. This is how reactive metals are extracted, how objects are electroplated, how batteries are recharged and how green hydrogen is made.

A galvanic cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy through a spontaneous reaction. An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy from a power supply to force a non-spontaneous reaction. In both, oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode. The polarity is opposite: in an electrolytic cell the anode is positive (connected to the positive terminal) and the cathode is negative.
Electrolytic cells usually have both electrodes in one container, because the reactants do not react spontaneously with each other.

List every species present, including water and the electrode material if it is not inert. On the electrochemical series, the strongest oxidising agent present is reduced at the cathode, and the strongest reducing agent present is oxidised at the anode.

Molten NaCl: Na⁺ is reduced to Na and Cl⁻ is oxidised to Cl₂. Dilute aqueous NaCl: water is a stronger oxidising agent than Na⁺, so hydrogen and OH⁻ form at the cathode; water is the stronger reducing agent, so oxygen forms at the anode. In concentrated NaCl solution, chlorine is produced at the anode instead, because the conditions are far from standard. This is why very reactive metals such as sodium and aluminium must be produced from molten electrolytes.

The amount of substance produced is proportional to the charge passed. \(Q = It\), \(n(e^-) = \dfrac{Q}{F}\) with \(F = 96\,500\ \mathrm{C\ mol^{-1}}\), then use the half-equation to relate electrons to product.
What mass of copper is deposited when 2.50 A flows for 30.0 minutes through CuSO₄ solution?

\(Q = 2.50 \times 1800 = 4500\ \mathrm{C}\). \(n(e^-) = \dfrac{4500}{96\,500} = 0.0466\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}\), so \(n(\mathrm{Cu}) = 0.0233\ \mathrm{mol}\) and \(m = 0.0233 \times 63.5 = 1.48\ \mathrm{g}\).

A rechargeable cell is a galvanic cell while discharging and an electrolytic cell while recharging. For this to work the discharge products must stay in contact with the electrodes so the reactions can be reversed. On recharge, the electrode that was the anode (−) becomes the cathode (−): the polarity stays, the process reverses. Battery life falls with side reactions, loss of contact of materials from the electrodes, and high or low temperatures.

Electrolysis of water gives hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. If the electricity comes from renewable sources, the product is called green hydrogen. Polymer electrolyte membrane electrolysers are one technology for this, and artificial photosynthesis is being developed to use sunlight to split water directly.

A power supply pushes electrons onto one electrode, making it negative. Positive ions are attracted to it and are reduced, so it is the cathode. The other electrode is positive; reducing agents give up electrons there, so it is the anode. The applied voltage must be greater than the voltage the reverse (galvanic) reaction would produce.

Inert electrodes (graphite, platinum) do not take part. A reactive metal anode may itself be oxidised: with a copper anode in copper(II) sulfate solution, Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ occurs at the anode in preference to water.
check: In an electrolytic cell, what is the polarity of the cathode and what happens there?
The cathode is negative, and reduction occurs there.

p: Molten magnesium chloride with inert electrodes. Species: Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ only. Cathode: Mg²⁺(l) + 2e⁻ → Mg(l). Anode: 2Cl⁻(l) → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻.

Aqueous copper(II) sulfate with inert electrodes. Species: Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H₂O. Oxidising agents: Cu²⁺ (+0.34 V) and H₂O (−0.83 V); the stronger is Cu²⁺, so Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) at the cathode. Reducing agent: water, so 2H₂O(l) → O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ at the anode. The solution becomes more acidic and its blue colour fades.

Aqueous potassium iodide. Cathode: water is a stronger oxidising agent than K⁺, so 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq). Anode: I⁻ (+0.54 V) is a stronger reducing agent than water (+1.23 V), so 2I⁻(aq) → I₂(aq) + 2e⁻.
check: What is produced at the cathode when aqueous sodium sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes?
Hydrogen gas (and hydroxide ions). Water is a stronger oxidising agent than Na⁺.

p: To plate an object with silver, make the object the cathode and a piece of silver the anode, in a solution containing Ag⁺. At the cathode Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s) coats the object; at the anode Ag(s) → Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ replaces the ions, so the concentration of the solution stays constant.

Finding time: how long must 5.00 A flow to deposit 2.70 g of aluminium from molten \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\)? \(n(\mathrm{Al}) = \dfrac{2.70}{27.0} = 0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(\mathrm{Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al}\), so \(n(e^-) = 0.300\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(Q = 0.300 \times 96\,500 = 28\,950\ \mathrm{C}\). \(t = \dfrac{Q}{I} = 5790\ \mathrm{s}\), about 96.5 minutes.
Finding the charge on an ion: 0.0100 mol of a metal is deposited by 2895 C. \(n(e^-) = \dfrac{2895}{96\,500} = 0.0300\ \mathrm{mol}\), three electrons per ion, so the ion is 3+.
Gas volume: 0.200 mol of electrons passes through water. Cathode: \(\mathrm{2H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2 + 2OH^-}\), so \(n(\mathrm{H_2}) = 0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\), which is 2.48 L at SLC.
check: How many moles of electrons are carried by a charge of 19 300 C?

topics.title: Organic structure and naming
points: Functional groups: alkene, haloalkane, hydroxyl (alcohol), amino (amine), carbonyl (aldehyde, ketone), carboxyl (carboxylic acid), ester, amide.
IUPAC naming: longest chain with the main functional group, lowest locants, substituents alphabetical.
Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols depend on how many carbons are bonded to the C–OH carbon.
Structural isomers differ in chain, position or functional group. Stereoisomers include cis–trans (around C=C) and optical isomers (a chiral carbon with four different groups).
Boiling point rises with chain length (dispersion forces) and with hydrogen bonding (alcohols, carboxylic acids, amines).
topics.explain: Explain why butan-1-ol has a higher boiling point than butanal.

qs.q: Which functional group is in an ester?
Propan-2-ol is a…
qs.e: The C–OH carbon is bonded to two other carbons.

qs.q: What makes a carbon atom chiral?
qs.a: It is bonded to four different groups, so its mirror images cannot be superimposed (optical isomers).

qs.q: Name CH₃CH₂COOCH₃.
qs.e: Alcohol part (methyl) first, acid part (propanoate) second.

qs.q: CH₃CH₂COOH is named…
Is butan-2-ol a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol?
A chiral centre is a carbon atom bonded to…
Name the ester formed from methanol and ethanoic acid.

p: Before this lesson you should know the alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids from Unit 1, and the types of intermolecular forces.

The big idea: an organic molecule is a carbon skeleton with one or more functional groups attached. The functional group decides how the molecule reacts, and the whole structure decides its physical properties. Systematic names let any chemist draw the exact molecule from its name.

Alkene: C=C. Haloalkane: –Cl, –Br, –I. Alcohol: hydroxyl, –OH. Aldehyde: –CHO at the end of a chain. Ketone: C=O within a chain. Carboxylic acid: carboxyl, –COOH. Primary amine: amino, –NH₂. Primary amide: –CONH₂. Ester: –COO– linking two carbon chains.
The functional group decides the chemical reactions; the carbon chain mainly affects physical properties.

fig.cap: Functional groups, their naming and an example.
head: Group
Structure
Name ending
Example

p: Choose the longest chain containing the principal functional group and number it so that group has the lowest number. The carboxylic acid group has the highest priority, then aldehyde and ketone, then hydroxyl, then amino; alkenes and halogens follow. A lower-priority group is named as a prefix: hydroxy- for –OH, amino- for –NH₂.
Examples: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂COOH is 3-hydroxybutanoic acid. CH₃COCH₂CH₃ is butan-2-one. CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ is methyl propanoate: the first word comes from the alcohol and the second from the carboxylic acid.

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but atoms connected in a different order: chain isomers (different branching), positional isomers (functional group in a different position) and functional isomers (different functional group, such as an alcohol and an ether, or an aldehyde and a ketone).

Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but a different arrangement in space. Cis–trans isomers occur around a C=C double bond when each carbon of the double bond has two different groups; the double bond cannot rotate. Optical isomers (enantiomers) are non-superimposable mirror images. They occur when a molecule has a chiral centre: a carbon atom attached to four different groups.
check: Can but-1-ene show cis–trans isomerism?
No. Carbon 1 has two identical hydrogen atoms attached. But-2-ene can.

p: Does butan-2-ol have a chiral centre?
Carbon 2 is attached to H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃. These are four different groups, so it is a chiral centre and butan-2-ol exists as two enantiomers. Butan-1-ol has no carbon with four different groups.

Boiling point depends on the strength of intermolecular forces: carboxylic acids (which form hydrogen-bonded pairs) are above alcohols and amides, which are above aldehydes, ketones and esters (dipole–dipole), which are above alkanes of similar molar mass (dispersion only). Solubility in water falls as the hydrocarbon chain lengthens. Viscosity rises with chain length and with hydrogen bonding.
CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂OH: longest chain containing the OH has four carbons (butan-); OH on carbon 1; methyl on carbon 2. Name: 2-methylbutan-1-ol.
CH₃CHClCH=CH₂: four carbons with a double bond; number from the end nearest the double bond, so it starts at carbon 1 and chlorine is on carbon 3. Name: 3-chlorobut-1-ene.
CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂: propan-1-amine. CH₃CH₂CONH₂: propanamide. CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO: butanal (the aldehyde carbon is always carbon 1, so no number is needed). HCOOCH₂CH₃: ethyl methanoate.
Cyclic and aromatic: cyclohexane is a ring of six CH₂ groups, C₆H₁₂. Benzene, C₆H₆, is a planar ring with delocalised electrons, drawn as a hexagon with a circle.
check: Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂COOH.
3-methylbutanoic acid. The carboxyl carbon is carbon 1 of a four-carbon chain.

p: Look at the carbon carrying the functional group and count the carbon atoms attached to it. One: primary (butan-1-ol). Two: secondary (butan-2-ol). Three: tertiary (2-methylpropan-2-ol). The class matters because it decides the product of oxidation in the next lesson.
check: Is propan-2-ol a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol?
Secondary: the carbon bearing the OH is attached to two other carbon atoms.

p: Example, C₄H₁₀O. Alcohols: butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol. All four are structural isomers; butan-2-ol also has a chiral centre.

Example, C₃H₆O₂: propanoic acid, methyl ethanoate and ethyl methanoate are functional isomers. The acid can form hydrogen bonds between its molecules, so it has a much higher boiling point than the esters.

Question: explain why butan-1-ol (118 °C) has a higher boiling point than butanal (75 °C) although their molar masses are similar. Answer: “Both have similar dispersion forces because they have similar numbers of electrons. Butanal is polar and has dipole–dipole attractions between molecules. Butan-1-ol has an O–H group, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, which are stronger than dipole–dipole attractions and require more energy to overcome.”
Flashpoint, the lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to ignite, follows the same reasoning: stronger intermolecular forces mean lower volatility and a higher flashpoint.

Including the carbon of –COOH or –CHO as a substituent instead of carbon 1 of the chain. Saying a molecule shows cis–trans isomerism when one double-bond carbon has two identical groups. Counting CH₃ and CH₂CH₃ as the same group.

topics.title: Organic reactions and pathways
points: Alkanes + halogens (UV): substitution → haloalkane. Haloalkane + OH⁻ → alcohol; haloalkane + NH₃ → amine.
Alkenes: addition of H₂ (Ni catalyst), halogens, HX, or H₂O (H₃PO₄ catalyst) → alcohol.
Primary alcohols oxidise (acidified Cr₂O₇²⁻ or MnO₄⁻) to aldehydes then carboxylic acids; secondary alcohols to ketones; tertiary alcohols do not oxidise.
Esterification: carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water (concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst).
\[\text{Atom economy} = \frac{\text{mass of desired product}}{\text{total mass of reactants}} \times 100\%\] \[\%\ \text{yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100\%\]
Green chemistry: high atom economy, renewable feedstocks, safer solvents, catalysts, less waste.
topics.explain: Draw the pathway from ethene to ethyl ethanoate and name every reagent.

qs.q: Oxidising propan-1-ol with acidified dichromate fully produces…
qs.e: Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid.

qs.q: Write the products of ethanoic acid + ethanol (H₂SO₄ catalyst).
qs.a: Ethyl ethanoate and water: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O

qs.q: \(0.80\ \mathrm{g}\) of product forms when \(1.00\ \mathrm{g}\) was theoretically possible. Find the percentage yield.
Which reaction has 100% atom economy?
qs.e: All reactant atoms end up in one product.

qs.q: Propan-1-ol is heated with excess acidified potassium dichromate. What is the organic product?
Ethene reacts with steam (acid catalyst) to form…
Find the atom economy for C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH.
qs.e: Addition: every reactant atom is in the product.

qs.q: A two-step synthesis has yields of 70% and 80%. Find the overall yield.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to name and draw organic molecules and classify alcohols as primary, secondary or tertiary.

The big idea: organic chemistry has a small number of reaction types, and each functional group can be converted into certain others. If you learn these conversions as a map, you can plan a route from a simple starting material to a target molecule, which is what synthetic chemists do.
Substitution: one atom or group replaces another. Alkane + Cl₂ in UV light gives a chloroalkane and HCl. A haloalkane with NaOH(aq) gives an alcohol; with NH₃ it gives an amine.
Addition: atoms add across a C=C double bond. With H₂ and a metal catalyst: alkane. With Br₂ or Cl₂: dihaloalkane. With HCl or HBr: haloalkane. With steam and an acid catalyst: alcohol.

Oxidation: a primary alcohol with acidified dichromate or permanganate gives an aldehyde, then a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone. A tertiary alcohol is not oxidised by these reagents. The orange dichromate turns green as it is reduced.

Condensation: two molecules join and release a small molecule. Carboxylic acid + alcohol gives an ester and water (concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst). Carboxylic acid + amine gives an amide and water. Hydrolysis is the reverse: water splits an ester into its acid and alcohol.
Work backwards from the product. Identify its functional group, ask what makes that group, and repeat until you reach the starting material.

Example: make ethyl ethanoate from ethene. The ester needs ethanol and ethanoic acid. Step 1: ethene + H₂O (H₃PO₄ catalyst, heat) → ethanol. Step 2: oxidise part of the ethanol with acidified Cr₂O₇²⁻ → ethanoic acid. Step 3: ethanol + ethanoic acid (concentrated H₂SO₄, heat) ⇌ ethyl ethanoate + water.

\(\%\ \text{yield} = \dfrac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100\). For a multi-step pathway the overall yield is the product of the yields of each step: steps of 80% and 60% give \(0.80 \times 0.60 = 48\%\).

Atom economy measures how much of the reactants’ mass ends up in the desired product. Addition reactions have 100% atom economy; substitution and condensation reactions are lower because they form a by-product. A reaction can have a high yield and still a poor atom economy.
check: A three-step synthesis has yields of 90%, 80% and 50%. What is the overall yield?

p: Find the atom economy for making ethanol (M = 46.0) by fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ (M of glucose = 180.0).
\(\text{Atom economy} = \dfrac{2 \times 46.0}{180.0} \times 100 = 51.1\%\). Hydration of ethene gives 100%, although it relies on a fossil-fuel feedstock.

Alkane → haloalkane (halogen, UV light; substitution). Alkene → alkane (H₂, catalyst), haloalkane (HCl or HBr), dihaloalkane (Br₂ or Cl₂) or alcohol (H₂O, acid catalyst). Haloalkane → alcohol (NaOH or KOH in water) or amine (NH₃). Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄). Secondary alcohol → ketone. Alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + water. Carboxylic acid + amine → amide + water. Ester + water → alcohol + carboxylic acid (hydrolysis).
Most pathway questions are solved by finding the two or three arrows on this map that connect the start to the target.
check: What reagents convert a haloalkane into an alcohol?
Aqueous sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide (a substitution reaction).

fig.cap: Reaction map: arrows show conversions you can use to plan a pathway. Alcohols are the central hub.

p: Substitution: CH₃CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃CH₂Cl + HCl. Addition: CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ (the major product) or CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. Substitution: CH₃CH₂Cl + NaOH → CH₃CH₂OH + NaCl. Substitution: CH₃CH₂Cl + NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HCl.

Oxidation of an alcohol in acid, written as a half-equation: CH₃CH₂OH(aq) + H₂O(l) → CH₃COOH(aq) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻. The oxidising agent’s half-equation is Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + 14H⁺(aq) + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺(aq) + 7H₂O(l).
Hydrolysis of an ester: CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH. Transesterification makes biodiesel: a triglyceride + 3 methanol → glycerol + 3 fatty acid methyl esters, with a base catalyst.
check: What organic product forms when butan-2-ol is heated with acidified potassium dichromate?
Butan-2-one, a ketone. Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones.

p: Target: propyl propanoate from propene as the only organic starting material. The ester needs propan-1-ol and propanoic acid. Step 1: propene + HCl → 1-chloropropane (with 2-chloropropane as the other product). Step 2: 1-chloropropane + NaOH(aq) → propan-1-ol. Step 3: oxidise half the propan-1-ol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ → propanoic acid. Step 4: propan-1-ol + propanoic acid, concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst and heat → propyl propanoate + water.
In practice each step is followed by separating and purifying the product, for example by fractional distillation, which separates liquids by boiling point.

fig.cap: Planning propyl propanoate from propene.

p: The same reaction types build and break the molecules in food. Condensation joins amino acids into proteins (amide, or peptide, links), monosaccharides into polysaccharides (glycosidic links) and glycerol with fatty acids into triglycerides (ester links), releasing water each time. Hydrolysis in digestion reverses each one, using water and enzymes.

Leaving out reagents and conditions on the arrow. Oxidising a tertiary alcohol. Writing esterification with a single arrow or without water as a product. Adding the percentage yields of steps instead of multiplying.

topics.title: Food chemistry and biomolecules
points: Proteins: amino acids join by condensation, forming peptide (amide) links and releasing water. Structure: primary to quaternary.
Carbohydrates: glucose units join by condensation (glycosidic links) into starch, glycogen and cellulose.
Fats and oils (triglycerides): glycerol + 3 fatty acids, joined by ester links. Unsaturated fats have C=C and lower melting points.
Hydrolysis is the reverse: water breaks the links during digestion, catalysed by enzymes.
Enzymes are protein catalysts with an active site. High temperature or extreme pH denatures them (the shape changes).
Energy values: carbohydrates and proteins about 17 kJ g⁻¹, fats about 37 kJ g⁻¹.
topics.explain: Explain why boiling denatures an enzyme but does not break its primary structure.

qs.q: The link between amino acids in a protein is a…
Hydrolysis of a triglyceride produces…
Why does an enzyme stop working at very low pH?
qs.a: Changes in pH disrupt the hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions holding the tertiary structure, so the active site changes shape (denatures) and the substrate no longer fits.

qs.q: Amino acids in a protein are joined by…
Fat provides about 37 kJ g⁻¹. How much energy is in 10 g of fat?
Saturated fats are solid at room temperature because…
o: their straight chains pack closely, giving stronger dispersion forces

qs.q: What is the difference between denaturing and hydrolysing a protein?
qs.a: Denaturing changes the shape (secondary and tertiary structure) without breaking peptide links. Hydrolysis breaks the peptide links into amino acids.

qs.q: Vitamin C is water-soluble because…
o: it has several –OH groups that hydrogen bond with water

p: Before this lesson you should know the functional groups, condensation and hydrolysis reactions, and intermolecular forces.

The big idea: the large molecules in food and in living things are polymers or assemblies built from small units by condensation reactions. Their properties, including how enzymes work and how much energy food supplies, follow from their structure and bonding.

Amino acids have an amino group and a carboxyl group on the same carbon, plus a side chain that varies. In solution they exist as zwitterions, with –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻. At low pH the molecule carries an overall positive charge; at high pH, negative.

Primary structure: the order of amino acids, held by covalent peptide (amide) links. Secondary structure: coils (alpha helices) and pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N–H groups of the backbone. Tertiary structure: the overall three-dimensional shape, held by interactions between side chains: hydrogen bonds, dipole–dipole and dispersion forces, ionic attractions and covalent disulfide bridges. Quaternary structure: two or more chains together.

Enzymes are protein catalysts. The substrate fits the active site (lock-and-key or induced fit), which is why each enzyme is specific. Heating above the optimum temperature, or changing pH, disrupts the bonds holding the tertiary structure; the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured. Denaturation leaves the primary structure intact. Hydrolysis, in contrast, breaks the peptide links.
Low temperatures slow enzymes without denaturing them. Coenzymes are small molecules that bind to an enzyme and help it function; many vitamins act this way.
check: An enzyme is heated to 80 °C and stops working. Which level of protein structure is unchanged?
The primary structure. Denaturation disrupts the secondary and tertiary structures but does not break peptide links.

p: Monosaccharides such as glucose join by condensation, forming glycosidic (ether) links and water. Starch is the energy store of plants: amylose is a mostly unbranched coil and amylopectin is branched. Glycogen is the more highly branched store in animals. Cellulose is a straight chain made of a different form of glucose; its chains hydrogen-bond into strong fibres, and humans lack the enzyme to hydrolyse it, so it acts as dietary fibre.
Glycaemic index (GI) ranks how quickly a food raises blood glucose. Amylopectin and simple sugars are digested quickly (high GI); amylose is digested slowly (lower GI).

A triglyceride forms when glycerol reacts with three fatty acids, making three ester links and three water molecules. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C bonds; their straight chains pack closely, giving stronger dispersion forces and higher melting points (fats, solid). Unsaturated chains have C=C bonds that create kinks, so they pack poorly and melt lower (oils, liquid). Omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids are essential: the body cannot make them.
Oxidative rancidity: oxygen attacks the C=C bonds of unsaturated fats, producing unpleasant-smelling compounds. Antioxidants such as vitamin C and vitamin E slow it by being oxidised in preference.

Vitamin C has several hydroxyl groups, forms hydrogen bonds with water and is water-soluble, so it is not stored and must be eaten regularly. Vitamin D is mostly non-polar hydrocarbon, so it is fat-soluble and stored in fatty tissue.

The general structure of an amino acid is H₂N–CH(R)–COOH, where R is the side chain. Glycine has R = H; alanine has R = CH₃. When two join, the carboxyl group of one reacts with the amino group of the other, forming a –CO–NH– link and water. Two amino acids give a dipeptide; many give a polypeptide.

Two different amino acids can form two different dipeptides, depending on which supplies the carboxyl group: glycine–alanine is not the same molecule as alanine–glycine. To hydrolyse a peptide on paper, break each C–N bond of the amide link, adding OH to the carbon and H to the nitrogen.
check: How many water molecules are released when a tripeptide forms from three amino acids?
Two. One water molecule is released for each peptide link, and a tripeptide has two links.

fig.cap: Condensation joins two amino acids by a peptide (amide) link and releases water. Hydrolysis reverses it.

p: In neutral solution an amino acid is a zwitterion: ⁺H₃N–CH(R)–COO⁻. In acid the –COO⁻ group accepts a proton, giving ⁺H₃N–CH(R)–COOH, an overall positive ion. In base the –NH₃⁺ group loses a proton, giving H₂N–CH(R)–COO⁻, an overall negative ion. Side chains with their own acidic or basic groups also change charge, which is why pH affects the ionic interactions that hold an enzyme’s tertiary structure.
check: What is the overall charge on a simple amino acid such as glycine in a strongly acidic solution?
Positive. The amino group is protonated (–NH₃⁺) and the carboxyl group is in its uncharged form (–COOH).

p: Example: a snack contains 12 g of carbohydrate, 5.0 g of protein and 8.0 g of fat. Using 16 kJ g⁻¹ for carbohydrate, 17 for protein and 37 for fat: energy \(= 12 \times 16 + 5.0 \times 17 + 8.0 \times 37 = 192 + 85 + 296 = 573\ \mathrm{kJ}\). Use the values in your data book; they differ slightly between sources.

The energy content of a food can be measured by burning a sample in a bomb calorimeter. The value available to the body is lower, because not everything is digested: cellulose, for example, burns in a calorimeter but passes through humans undigested.

Proteins: monomers are amino acids; amide links; hydrolysed to amino acids, which are used to build new proteins. Carbohydrates: monomers are monosaccharides; glycosidic links; hydrolysed to glucose, the main fuel for respiration. Fats and oils: glycerol and three fatty acids; ester links; hydrolysed to glycerol and fatty acids; stored as an energy reserve. Fats are not polymers, because they are not made of a long chain of repeating units.

topics.title: Laboratory analysis of organic compounds
points: Test for C=C: bromine water turns from orange-brown to colourless (addition).
Test for a carboxylic acid: sodium carbonate or hydrogencarbonate gives bubbles of CO₂.
Primary and secondary alcohols and aldehydes are oxidised by acidified dichromate (orange to green); tertiary alcohols and ketones are not.
Purity: a pure solid has a sharp melting point; impurities lower it and widen the range.
Volumetric analysis, including redox titrations, measures the amount of an organic compound; simple and fractional distillation separate and purify liquids.
topics.explain: You are given three unlabelled colourless liquids: hex-1-ene, propanoic acid and butan-2-ol. Describe how you would identify each with simple tests.

p: Before this lesson you should know the functional groups and their reactions, redox half-equations and titration calculations.

The big idea: before using instruments, a chemist can learn a lot about an organic compound with quick tests in a test tube, check its purity with a melting point, purify it by distillation and measure how much is present by titration. These methods rely on the characteristic reactions of functional groups.

Carbon–carbon double bond: add a few drops of bromine water and shake. An alkene decolourises it quickly at room temperature, because bromine adds across the double bond. An alkane does not react without UV light, so the colour remains.

Carboxyl group: add sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate. Fizzing shows carbon dioxide, because the acid is strong enough to react with carbonate: 2CH₃COOH(aq) + Na₂CO₃(aq) → 2CH₃COONa(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Blue litmus turning red also indicates an acid.

Hydroxyl group: warm with acidified potassium dichromate. Primary and secondary alcohols are oxidised and the solution turns from orange (Cr₂O₇²⁻) to green (Cr³⁺). Tertiary alcohols give no change. Aldehydes are also oxidised by this reagent, whereas ketones are not, which distinguishes those two families.
check: A compound decolourises bromine water and also fizzes with sodium carbonate. What two functional groups does it contain?
A carbon–carbon double bond and a carboxyl group.
Which will not change the colour of acidified dichromate: propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol or 2-methylpropan-2-ol?
2-methylpropan-2-ol, because it is a tertiary alcohol.

Detects
Positive result

p: A pure crystalline solid melts sharply, over a range of about 1 °C, at a temperature that can be looked up. Impurities disrupt the regular packing of the lattice, so less energy is needed to break it apart: the melting point is lower and the solid melts over a wider range.

Example: pure aspirin melts at about 135 °C. A sample that melts between 126 and 131 °C is impure. A mixed melting point test confirms identity: mixing the sample with a known pure sample of the suspected compound leaves the melting point unchanged only if they are the same substance.

Simple distillation separates a liquid from dissolved solids, or two liquids with very different boiling points. The mixture is heated, the more volatile component vaporises first, and the vapour is cooled in a condenser and collected.

Fractional distillation separates liquids with closer boiling points. A fractionating column between the flask and the condenser gives the vapour a large surface on which to condense and re-evaporate many times. Each cycle enriches the vapour in the component with the lower boiling point, so that component reaches the top first. The thermometer at the top shows which fraction is being collected.
check: In fractional distillation of a mixture of ethanol (78 °C) and water (100 °C), which is collected first?
Ethanol, because it has the lower boiling point and is more volatile.

p: Acid–base titration measures organic acids, for example the ethanoic acid in vinegar or the acid content of fruit juice, using standard sodium hydroxide and phenolphthalein.

Redox titration measures compounds that can be oxidised or reduced. Ethanol in wine can be oxidised by a standard dichromate solution; vitamin C (ascorbic acid) can be titrated with standard iodine solution, using starch as an indicator that turns blue-black at the end point: C₆H₈O₆(aq) + I₂(aq) → C₆H₆O₆(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq). Permanganate is self-indicating: the first permanent pale pink marks the end point.

notes.h: Worked example: vitamin C in juice
p: A 25.00 mL sample of juice is titrated with 0.00500 M iodine solution; the average titre is 18.40 mL. Find the mass of vitamin C (M = 176.0 g mol⁻¹) per 100 mL.

\(n(\mathrm{I_2}) = 0.00500 \times 0.01840 = 9.20 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol}\). The ratio is 1 : 1, so \(n(\text{vitamin C}) = 9.20 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol}\) in 25.00 mL. \(m = 9.20 \times 10^{-5} \times 176.0 = 0.0162\ \mathrm{g}\). Per 100 mL: \(0.0162 \times 4 = 0.0648\ \mathrm{g} = 64.8\ \mathrm{mg}\).

The amount of iodine or bromine that reacts with a fat or oil measures how many C=C bonds it contains, because each double bond adds one molecule of halogen. The more halogen that reacts per gram, the more unsaturated the oil.
Example: 0.010 mol of a fatty acid reacts with 0.030 mol of \(\mathrm{I_2}\). Each molecule therefore contains three C=C double bonds.

Writing that bromine water “goes clear”; say it is decolourised or turns colourless. Saying an impurity raises the melting point. Claiming dichromate distinguishes a primary from a secondary alcohol by colour: both turn it green. Forgetting the mole ratio in a redox titration.

qs.q: Which reagent distinguishes hexane from hex-1-ene?
qs.e: The alkene decolourises bromine water by addition; the alkane does not react.

qs.q: A solid melts between 112 °C and 118 °C. The pure compound melts at 122 °C. The sample is…
qs.e: Impurities lower the melting point and widen the range.

qs.q: Which compound gives a colour change from orange to green when warmed with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇?
qs.e: Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol and is oxidised to propanone.

qs.q: What would you observe when sodium hydrogencarbonate is added to ethanoic acid, and why?
qs.a: Bubbles of gas. The acid reacts with the hydrogencarbonate to produce carbon dioxide, water and sodium ethanoate.

qs.q: Why does a fractionating column improve the separation of two liquids?
qs.a: It provides a large surface area for repeated condensation and evaporation. Each cycle enriches the vapour in the more volatile component, so the liquids are separated more completely.

qs.q: 0.020 mol of an unsaturated fatty acid reacts with 0.040 mol of I₂. How many C=C bonds are in each molecule?
qs.e: Each double bond adds one I₂: 0.040 ÷ 0.020 = 2.

qs.q: How could acidified potassium dichromate distinguish propanal from propanone?
qs.a: Propanal (an aldehyde) is oxidised and turns the solution from orange to green; propanone (a ketone) does not.

topics.title: Spectroscopy and chromatography
points: Mass spectrometry: the molecular ion peak (M⁺) gives the molar mass; fragments help identify structure.
Infrared: O–H (alcohol) broad 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; O–H (acid) very broad 2500–3300; C=O sharp about 1700; C–H about 2850–3000.
¹³C NMR: the number of peaks equals the number of different carbon environments.
\({}^1\mathrm{H}\) NMR: number of peaks = proton environments; area ratio = relative number of H; splitting follows the \(n + 1\) rule.
HPLC: retention time identifies a compound; peak area (with a calibration curve) gives its concentration.
Redox titrations (e.g. with MnO₄⁻) and qualitative tests (bromine water for C=C) also identify and quantify organic compounds.

How many peaks would ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) show in its ¹³C NMR spectrum?
In ¹H NMR, a signal split into a triplet means the neighbouring carbon has…
In HPLC, a compound is identified by its…
qs.e: Peak area tells you how much.

qs.q: What does adding bromine water show about an organic compound?
qs.a: If the orange colour disappears quickly, the compound has a C=C double bond (an addition reaction occurs).

qs.q: In a mass spectrum, the molecular ion peak gives…
How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propanone, CH₃COCH₃?
qs.e: The two CH₃ carbons are equivalent.

qs.q: In ¹H NMR, what is the splitting pattern of a CH₃ group next to a CH₂ group?
A calibration curve gives absorbance \(A = [[k]] \times c\) (c in mg L⁻¹). A sample has absorbance [[A]]. Find its concentration in mg L⁻¹, to 2 decimal places.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to name and draw organic molecules, recognise functional groups and understand chromatography from Unit 1.

The big idea: chemists cannot see molecules, so they probe them with energy and read the response. Each instrument answers a different question. Put together, the answers identify a compound and how much of it is present. The skill being tested is combining several pieces of evidence into one structure.

Mass spectrometry: molar mass and fragments. Infrared spectroscopy: the functional groups present. Carbon-13 NMR: the number of different carbon environments. Proton NMR: the number of hydrogen environments, how many hydrogens are in each, and how many hydrogens are on neighbouring carbons. Chromatography: separation, identification and quantity. Structure questions give several spectra together, and each one narrows the possibilities.

Molecules are ionised and broken into positively charged fragments, which are separated by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z). The peak with the highest significant m/z is the molecular ion and gives the relative molecular mass. The tallest peak is the base peak, the most abundant fragment. Fragments are written with a positive charge: a peak at m/z 15 is CH₃⁺, 29 is CH₃CH₂⁺ or CHO⁺, 45 is COOH⁺. A difference of 15 from the molecular ion suggests loss of a methyl group. Small peaks one unit above the molecular ion come from carbon-13.
check: A mass spectrum has its last significant peak at m/z 46 and a large peak at m/z 31. Suggest the compound and the fragment lost.
Ethanol (M = 46). Loss of CH₃ (15) gives the fragment CH₂OH⁺ at m/z 31.

p: Covalent bonds absorb infrared radiation at characteristic wavenumbers and vibrate more strongly. Use the data book ranges. The most useful absorptions: a broad O–H band for alcohols; a very broad O–H band overlapping the C–H region for carboxylic acids; a strong, sharp C=O band near 1700 cm⁻¹; N–H bands for amines and amides. The region below about 1400 cm⁻¹ is the fingerprint region, unique to each compound.

p: Carbon-13 NMR: each peak is one carbon environment; chemical shift indicates the type of carbon. Use symmetry: propan-2-ol has two carbon environments, propan-1-ol has three.

Proton NMR gives four pieces of information. Number of signals: number of hydrogen environments. Chemical shift: the type of environment. Relative peak area: the ratio of hydrogens in each environment. Splitting: a signal is split into n + 1 peaks by n hydrogens on adjacent carbons. Hydrogens on O–H usually appear as a singlet.
A compound C₄H₈O₂ has an IR band near 1740 cm⁻¹ and no broad O–H band. Its proton NMR shows a singlet (3H) at 3.7 ppm, a quartet (2H) at 2.3 ppm and a triplet (3H) at 1.1 ppm.

The C=O band without an O–H band suggests an ester. A quartet (2H) with a triplet (3H) is an ethyl group, CH₃CH₂–. The singlet (3H) is a CH₃ with no hydrogens on the neighbouring atom. Two esters fit: methyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₃, and ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃. The chemical shifts decide. A singlet at 3.7 ppm is a CH₃ attached to oxygen, and a quartet at 2.3 ppm is a CH₂ next to C=O, so the compound is methyl propanoate. In ethyl ethanoate the quartet would be near 4.1 ppm (CH₂ attached to oxygen) and the singlet near 2.0 ppm.

Check: methyl propanoate has four carbon environments, so its carbon-13 spectrum should show four peaks, and its molecular ion should be at m/z 88. Always confirm the final structure against every piece of data.

In HPLC the sample is pumped at high pressure through a column packed with a stationary phase. Components that are more strongly attracted to the stationary phase take longer to pass through and have longer retention times. Retention time identifies a component when compared with a standard under the same conditions. The area under a peak is proportional to the amount; a calibration curve from standards gives the concentration.
Volumetric analysis, including redox titrations, measures the amount of a substance precisely. Purity can also be checked by melting point: an impure solid melts lower and over a wider range.

1. Mass spectrum: read the molecular ion to get the molar mass, and check it against any molecular formula given. 2. Infrared: decide which functional groups are present and, just as usefully, which are absent. 3. Carbon-13 NMR: count the carbon environments; fewer peaks than carbons means the molecule has symmetry. 4. Proton NMR: for each signal, record the shift, the relative number of hydrogens and the splitting, and build fragments such as CH₃CH₂– or (CH₃)₂CH–. 5. Join the fragments, then check the proposed structure against every piece of data.
check: An IR spectrum shows a strong band at 1700 cm⁻¹ and a very broad band from 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹. What functional group is present?
A carboxylic acid: the C=O band together with the very broad O–H (acid) band.

p: A triplet (3H) with a quartet (2H) is an ethyl group, CH₃CH₂–. A doublet (6H) with a septet (1H) is an isopropyl group, (CH₃)₂CH–. A singlet (3H) is a methyl group with no hydrogens on the neighbouring atom, such as CH₃–C=O or CH₃–O–. A singlet (9H) is three equivalent methyl groups, (CH₃)₃C–.

Example: propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. The two CH₃ groups are equivalent: a doublet (6H), split by the one hydrogen on the middle carbon. The CH is a septet (1H), split by six neighbours. The OH is a singlet (1H). Carbon-13 NMR shows two peaks. Propan-1-ol would show three carbon peaks and four proton signals.
check: How many peaks would the ¹³C NMR spectrum of 2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CH, show?
Two. The three CH₃ carbons are equivalent, and the central CH is the second environment.
