A C=O with no O–H means an aldehyde or ketone. One proton environment and two carbon environments mean a highly symmetrical molecule: propanone, CH₃COCH₃. The alternative, propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO), would give three carbon peaks and three proton signals.

Example: caffeine standards of 10, 20, 30 and 40 mg L⁻¹ give peak areas of 150, 300, 450 and 600 units. A drink diluted 1 in 10 gives a caffeine peak of area 375 at the same retention time. From the calibration line, 375 corresponds to 25 mg L⁻¹ in the diluted sample, so the drink contains 250 mg L⁻¹.

Changing the conditions changes retention times: a faster flow rate, a higher temperature or a shorter column makes all components come out sooner, which can reduce how well they are separated. In reverse-phase HPLC the stationary phase is non-polar and the mobile phase polar, so polar compounds come out first.

Using the tallest peak as the molecular ion. Leaving the positive charge off a fragment. Counting hydrogens on the same carbon when working out splitting. Reading a concentration off a calibration curve beyond its range.

topics.title: Medicinal chemistry
points: Many medicines come from plants. Active compounds are extracted with a solvent in which they are soluble, then purified by distillation or chromatography.
Enzymes are protein catalysts; a substrate binds at the active site, which is specific in shape and in the interactions it can form.
A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate and blocks the active site.
Enantiomers of a chiral drug can have different effects in the body, because receptors and enzymes are themselves chiral.
Structure determines function: functional groups decide how a medicine dissolves, binds and is broken down.
topics.explain: Explain why one enantiomer of a drug might be an effective medicine while its mirror image is not.

p: Before this lesson you should understand solubility and intermolecular forces, chirality, protein structure and enzymes.

The big idea: a medicine works because its molecules have the right shape and the right functional groups to bind to a particular target in the body, usually a protein. Medicinal chemistry applies everything in organic chemistry to finding, isolating, identifying and improving such molecules.

Plants make a huge range of organic compounds, and many medicines were first found in them. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have long used plants as medicines, and this knowledge has guided scientists to active compounds.

Solvent extraction: plant material is crushed and soaked in a solvent that dissolves the compound of interest. “Like dissolves like” guides the choice: a non-polar compound is extracted with a non-polar solvent such as hexane; a polar compound with water or ethanol. The solvent is then evaporated. Steam or simple distillation separates volatile oils such as eucalyptus oil. Chromatography separates and purifies individual components, and spectroscopy identifies their structures.
check: A plant compound has a long hydrocarbon chain and no polar groups. Would water or hexane be the better solvent to extract it?
Hexane. The compound is non-polar, so it dissolves in a non-polar solvent.

p: An enzyme is a protein whose tertiary structure creates a pocket called the active site. The substrate fits into it and is held by hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions, dipole–dipole and dispersion forces with the side chains that line it. In the lock-and-key model the substrate fits exactly; in the induced-fit model the active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds. Either way, binding provides a reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.

Enzymes are highly specific: because the active site is itself chiral, an enzyme will usually accept only one enantiomer of a substrate. Enzyme activity depends on temperature and pH. Activity rises with temperature up to an optimum, then falls sharply as the enzyme denatures. Each enzyme has an optimum pH; away from it, the charges on acidic and basic side chains change, disrupting the interactions that hold the active site in shape.

p: Many medicines work by slowing down a particular enzyme. A competitive inhibitor is a molecule similar enough in shape and functional groups to the substrate that it binds to the active site, but it does not react. While it is there, the substrate cannot bind, so the rate of the enzyme-catalysed reaction falls. Because inhibitor and substrate compete, raising the substrate concentration reduces the effect.
Designing an inhibitor means matching the active site: the right overall shape, and functional groups placed to form the same kinds of interactions as the natural substrate.
check: How does a competitive inhibitor reduce the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction?
It binds to the active site in place of the substrate, so fewer enzyme molecules are available to bind substrate at any moment.

p: Enantiomers have the same melting point, solubility and reactions with non-chiral reagents, but they interact differently with other chiral molecules. A receptor in the body is like a glove: a left hand fits it and a right hand does not. So one enantiomer of a drug may bind and act, while the other is inactive or binds somewhere else and causes side effects.

For this reason, medicines are often produced as a single enantiomer. This requires either a synthesis that makes only one, often using an enzyme as the catalyst, or separating the two after synthesis.
check: What structural feature makes a molecule chiral?
A carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups (a chiral centre), giving two non-superimposable mirror images.

notes.h: Reading the structure of a medicine
p: Given the structure of a drug, you may be asked to circle and name its functional groups, find chiral centres, predict solubility or suggest how it reacts. Polar groups such as –OH, –COOH and –NH₂ form hydrogen bonds with water and increase solubility in blood. Large non-polar regions make a molecule more soluble in fats, so it can cross cell membranes and be stored in fatty tissue.
Example: aspirin contains a carboxyl group, an ester group and a benzene ring. Its ester group can be hydrolysed, which is how it is broken down; its carboxyl group makes it a weak acid.

Saying enantiomers have different chemical formulas or different boiling points. Saying an inhibitor denatures the enzyme. Describing the active site as matching only in shape and forgetting the intermolecular interactions. Choosing an extraction solvent without referring to polarity.

o: breaks the peptide bonds of the enzyme
binds to the active site in place of the substrate
raises the activation energy of all reactions
is always the mirror image of the enzyme

qs.q: Two enantiomers differ in…
o: the order in which atoms are connected
qs.e: They are non-superimposable mirror images with the same connectivity.

qs.q: Which solvent is most suitable for extracting a polar compound with several –OH groups from leaves?
qs.e: Ethanol is polar and can form hydrogen bonds with the compound.

qs.q: Why might only one enantiomer of a drug be effective?
qs.a: The drug’s target (a receptor or enzyme) is chiral, so only the enantiomer with the matching three-dimensional arrangement can bind to it correctly.

qs.q: Explain why enzyme activity falls when the pH moves away from the optimum.
qs.a: The change in pH alters the charges on acidic and basic side chains, disrupting the ionic and hydrogen bonding that maintain the tertiary structure. The shape of the active site changes, so the substrate binds less well.

qs.q: An enzyme’s specificity comes from…
o: the shape of its active site and the interactions it can form

qs.q: Why does adding more substrate reduce the effect of a competitive inhibitor?
qs.a: Substrate and inhibitor compete for the same active site; more substrate makes it more likely the substrate binds.

topics.title: Investigations and exam technique
points: Practical investigation: question, hypothesis, variables, method, results, discussion of errors and conclusion, communicated as a scientific poster.
Know the data book: where each formula, constant and table is, and which values need care.
Command terms: identify (name), describe (give features), explain (give reasons), compare (similarities and differences), evaluate (judge with evidence), justify (support a choice).
Show working in calculations, carry units, and round only at the end to the correct significant figures.
Section A is multiple choice; Section B is short and extended answers. Allocate time by marks.
topics.explain: Take a past exam question you got wrong. Explain what the question was really asking and what a full-mark answer needed.

p: Read this lesson once you have covered most of Units 3 and 4, and return to it before each practice exam.

The big idea: knowing the chemistry is necessary but not enough. Marks are lost through misreading the question, missing a step in the working, or answers that describe when the question asks for an explanation. These are skills that improve quickly with deliberate practice.

In Unit 4 you design or adapt and conduct an investigation related to energy, the production of chemicals or organic compounds, and report it as a scientific poster. The usual sections are: title (often the research question), introduction (background chemistry and hypothesis), methodology and methods (what was done, with variables and safety), results (tables and graphs with units), discussion (trends, explanation, errors and their effects, improvements) and conclusion (answer to the question, linked to the evidence), plus references.

The highest marks go to the discussion. Link results to chemical concepts, be specific about the quality of the data (accuracy, precision, repeatability, validity), and say how each source of error would change the result and in which direction.

fig.cap: The sections of a scientific poster.

p: The data book supplies the periodic table, the electrochemical series, formulas and constants, heats of combustion, infrared ranges, NMR shifts, and structures of amino acids, fatty acids and vitamins. You do not need to memorise these, but you must find them quickly.

Points that catch students: heats of combustion are given as positive magnitudes, so supply the negative sign for ΔH yourself; molar volume applies only at SLC; the electrochemical series lists reductions at standard conditions; infrared and NMR values are ranges, so use them together with other evidence.
check: The data book lists the heat of combustion of methane as 890 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for the combustion equation?
−890 kJ mol⁻¹. Combustion is exothermic, so ΔH is negative.

p: Underline the command term and the number of marks. One mark usually needs one distinct, correct point. “Explain” requires a reason linked to a result: use “because” or “so”. “Compare” requires a statement about both things. “Evaluate” or “discuss” requires points on more than one side and a judgment.

Use the information in the question. If a question gives data about an unfamiliar battery or molecule, the answer is expected to refer to that particular system, not to a textbook example. Use correct chemical terms: “ionises completely”, not “breaks up fully”; “successful collisions”, not “more reactions”.

Write the formula, substitute with units, and state each intermediate answer. If you make an arithmetic slip, later marks can still be awarded for a correct method (consequential marks), but only if the working can be followed. Keep extra digits through the calculation and round the final answer to the number of significant figures in the least precise data. Check that the answer is reasonable: a pH of 15, a negative mass or a yield above 100% signals an error.
check: A calculation uses the data 25.00 mL, 0.105 M and 18.6 mL. How many significant figures should the answer have?
Three, matching the least precise values (0.105 and 18.6).

p: Spread revision out and test yourself; rereading notes feels productive but builds little recall. Use Review on this site daily. Do past exam questions by topic first, then complete papers under timed conditions. After marking, sort every lost mark into one of three groups: did not know the content, misread the question, or made a slip. Fix the first with study, the second by underlining command terms, and the third by checking units and significant figures.
Read the examiners’ reports that are published with past exams. They show exactly what earned marks and the errors that were most common.

Writing everything you know about a topic and hoping some of it is relevant. Leaving multiple-choice questions blank. Giving one point for a three-mark question. Omitting states in equations. Spending too long on one hard question and running out of time for easier marks.

qs.q: A question says “Explain why the rate increases.” The answer must include…
o: only a statement that it increases
a reason linked to the change
qs.e: “Explain” asks for the reason.

qs.q: Which section of a scientific poster should discuss sources of error and their effect on the results?
What are consequential marks, and how do you make sure you can earn them?
qs.a: Marks awarded for a correct method that follows from an earlier wrong value. You earn them by showing clear working at every step.

qs.q: After marking a practice exam, into which three groups should you sort lost marks?
qs.a: Content you did not know, questions you misread, and slips such as arithmetic, units or significant figures.

qs.q: The molar volume of 24.8 L mol⁻¹ can be used for…
The data book gives the heat of combustion of propane as 2220 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH for its combustion is…
qs.e: Combustion is exothermic.

qs.q: What must an answer to an “explain” question include?
qs.a: A reason linked to the result, not just a description.

qs.q: How many significant figures does 0.0250 have?
qs.e: Leading zeros do not count; the trailing zero does.
